Abstract
Healthcare 4.0 is considered to be the most resilient technology with the integration of Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial 
Intelligence (AI), and 5G wireless communication. These Internet-enabled devices compile human data and deliver it 
to remote clinical centers for efficient diagnosis and treatment processes. Though sensor-driven devices have largely 
eased everyday lives, these healthcare systems have been suffering from various security breaches and data privacy 
problems. This evokes a need for designing intelligent systems to eradicate data breaches and privacy problems. This 
research presents a groundbreaking framework that uniquely combines privacy-preserving optimized deep learning to 
effectively diagnose cardiac troubles utilizing edge and fog computing devices. The recommended framework is tested 
with real-time datasets and employs federated learning for training the network. To ensure high prediction performance, 
Gated Aquila Optimized Deep Feedforward Networks (GAODP) are used to predict heart diseases. In the primary instance, 
information is acquired by the IoT sensors and stored in fog gateways. Subsequently, the federated mode of GAODP is 
adopted for the prediction of heart diseases. The ablation tests are conducted utilizing IoT nodes connected to medical 
sensors, with fog gateways implemented using Embedded Jetson Nano gadgets. Extensive evaluations are carried out 
using the gathered datasets, and performance metrics are examined and analyzed. The experimentation involves various 
traditional deep learning frameworks to prove the performance of privacy-preserving models. Moreover, the duration 
required to construct the model is calculated to confirm the recommended model’s intricacy. The outcome indicate that 
the recommended model has attained notable predictive accuracy, including precision (0.98), recall (0.975), specificity 
(0.98), F1-score (0.99) and accuracy (0.99) with less computational overhead.

1  Introduction
Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain a leading cause of mortality worldwide, with an estimated 17.9 million deaths 
annually, accounting for approximately 32% of global deaths [1]. The Global Burden of Disease (GBD) research highlights 
that in India, the mortality rate due to cardiac illness stands at 272 per 100,000 individuals, significantly surpassing the 
universal mean of 235 per 100,000 [2]. The prevalence of cardiac diseases in India is particularly alarming in impoverished 
and rural regions, where healthcare accessibility is limited, leading to delays in diagnosis and treatment. Additionally, 
the rising burden of cardiac conditions is driven by factors such as sedentary lifestyles, increasing prevalence of diabetes 
and hypertension, poor dietary habits, and inadequate medical infrastructure [3].
Early detection and timely intervention are crucial in reducing premature mortality from cardiac conditions. Conven-
tional diagnostic techniques, such as electrocardiograms (ECG), echocardiography, and cardiac MRIs, require specialized 
expertise and are often inaccessible in resource-constrained settings [4]. The lack of accurate, cost-effective, and scalable 
diagnostic solutions further exacerbates the issue. Consequently, developing intelligent predictive models that offer 
real-time diagnosis and decision support is imperative. However, creating such systems presents challenges, including 
handling large-scale medical data, ensuring prediction accuracy, and maintaining interpretability [5].
The integration of emerging technologies like the IoT, edge computing, and fog computing has shown promise in 
elevating predictive performance. The synergy between IoT and distributed computing paradigms enables real-time data 
analysis, reducing dependence on centralized cloud-based systems [6]. Particularly, fog computing offers advantages 
such as low latency, privacy preservation, improved security, and optimized network bandwidth, making it suitable for 
healthcare applications requiring immediate response [7–9].
While AI techniques, comprising DL and ML approaches, have demonstrated success in medical diagnostics, they often 
rely on extensive datasets sourced from a single institution [10, 11]. However, training deep learning models with limited 
datasets leads to feature bias, reducing model generalizability and increasing misclassification rates. A viable solution 
to this issue is collaborative learning, where multiple hospitals share anonymized patient data to enhance predictive 
accuracy. However, concerns regarding data security, patient privacy, and regulatory constraints hinder data-sharing 
practices [12, 13].
This research study introduces an incorporated fog/edge-based privacy-preserving model designed to deliver superior 
detection performance, minimal latency, efficient resource usage, and enhanced security for those having cardiovascular 
issues and others needing real-time capabilities. The proposed model works in three different phases: data collection 
phase, federated (privacy-preserving) training model, and prediction phase.
To the best of our understanding, this paper represents the initial implementation of privacy-preserving learning 
models on fog devices without sacrificing performance or efficacy. The main contributions of this study include:
1.	 Created simplified Gated Recurrent Units(GRU) combined with Feedforward Learning Networks, tailored for effective 
use in fog computing devices.
2.	 Recommended Enhanced Aquila Optimization to tune the hyperparameters of feedforward learning networks, reduc-
ing the duration for constructing the algorithm and latency in predicting heart diseases.
3.	 Proposed a privacy-preserving and collaborative training model for the proposed networks.
4.	 Developed experimental environments for real-time data acquisition networks utilizing Embedded Jetson Nano 
boards.
5.	 Assessed the functionality of the proposed model on these custom-built test environments. The collaborative learn-
ing model outperformed alternative models and was evaluated against various cutting-edge DL approaches.

2  Background works
Kumar et al. [14] suggest a novel IoT-enabled intelligent agriculture system for safe data swap among its numerous actors 
using deep learning and blockchain technology. To guarantee safe data transmit in IoT-enabled IA, this method initially 
developed an innovative authentication and key management framework. Subsequently, the cloud server employs an 
advanced deep learning model to detect and identify additional breaches through encrypted transactions. However, 
this architecture is not appropriate for live setting [14].
Tan et al. [15] integrated two-layered Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) with lightweight cryptography techniques 
to provide defensive characteristics in the IoT-Cloud-Edge Collaborative environment. The authors designed intelligent 
systems to safeguard cloud data against Man-In-The-Middle (MIM) attacks. The promising results showcased an accuracy 
of 96%, proving the performance of the recommended model can fit IoT-Cloud-Edge environments [15].
Syed Mohamed et al. [16] present an advanced IDS framework devised specifically for multi-cloud IoT environments. 
Extensive testing on real-world datasets demonstrates the framework’s high accuracy and efficiency in identifying a 
wide range of intrusion types. The results indicate that the swarm-based approach significantly enhances the detection 
performance compared to traditional methods, ensuring a secure and resilient IoT infrastructure [16].
Zhuo Chen et al. [17] recommend an IDS utilizing federated learning approaches. Unlike traditional centralized learn-
ing methods, FedAGRU updates collective learning models instead of directly sending unprocessed data along with 
edge devices and a central server [17].
Preuveneers et al. [18] introduced an iterative enhancement to an anomaly-based learning algorithm, integrating 
it within a distributed ledger framework through a permissioned blockchain-based federated learning approach. This 
procedure empowers the auditing of ML models without centralizing training data, by merging federated learning and 
blockchain technologies [18]. This increase in model complexity extends computational time and poses challenges for 
real-time applications.
Nguyen et al. [19] identified a novel data poisoning strategy enabling an attacker to implant a backdoor within consoli-
dated detection model, resulting in malicious traffic being incorrectly classified like benign [19]. By utilizing compromised 
IoT devices instead of traditional gateways or clients, the attacker can avoid detection. Their experiments with 46 IoT 
devices demonstrated the efficacy of this method in embedding backdoors and evading advanced FL poisoning defenses.
Despite advancements in IoT-enabled healthcare, existing methods struggle to balance privacy, efficiency, and real-
time accuracy. Centralized models often compromise data privacy and security, while complex architectures increase 
latency and computational demands, limiting their use in resource-constrained settings. Thus, there is a critical need 
for a privacy-preserving, lightweight, and efficient framework that integrates edge and fog computing with optimized 
deep learning models to enhance real-time cardiac disease prediction. This study addresses these gaps by proposing a 
federated, privacy-preserving model optimized for fog devices (Fig. 1) (Table 1).
3  Proposed methodology
3.1  Data collection unit
Assessing efficacy of the proposed model, a cohort of approximately 60 individuals, ranging in age from 22 to 65, was 
selected. This group is evenly split between healthy participants and those experiencing moderate heart disease. The 
study employs IoT technology to collect heart signal data from the volunteers. Electrocardiography (ECG) sensors are 
utilized then connected to NodeMCU and MCP3008 boards, which capture the ECG signals from the subjects and transmit 
data to nearby edge devices equipped with NVIDIA Jetson Nano boards. In cases where the 3.3 V batteries deplete, fresh 
batteries may be used to maintain power for the IoT devices. In addition to ECG data collection, blood pressure measure-
ments are taken and used as reference values to address missing data during the preprocessing phase. Furthermore, the 
NVIDIA Jetson Nano boards, which are Wi-Fi-enabled, serve as Fog gateways, and the final output information is retained

To train and evaluate the proposed algorithm, a total of 1672 datasets were collected. Out of these, 887 were categorized

among various training and testing proportions for optimizing the algorithm.
3.2  Data pre‑processing and preparation
Ascertain values for different attributes, it is essential to preprocess the data from ECG and blood pressure sensors before 
inputting it into a deep learning model [20–22]. This preprocessing requires incorporating domain-specific knowledge 
pertinent to the application. Due to significant skew in the data, normalization is necessary. Blood Pressure (BP) data is 
similarly skewed, with higher readings (greater than 130/100) observed in individuals with heart disease compared to 
those without. Healthy patients’ heartbeat distributions are leptokurtic, while patients with abnormal heartbeats show 
target-oriented patterns. At their maximum, healthy individuals record a higher heart rate (approximately 160) contrasted 
to individuals with heart disease (around 150). The preprocessed data are then used in the training and testing phases 
to determine the condition of the patient’s heart.

3.3  Hybrid deep learning model
This section within the architecture utilizes pre-processed data to train the recommended hybrid framework. The data, 
sourced from BAN-IoT nodes affixed to patients’ bodies, are then processed using a hybrid deep learning approach. This 
approach integrates self-attention-relied gated units with a Logistics Chaos-optimized Aquila feed-forward learning 
network.
3.4  Feed forward learning networks
The fully connected layers employ the Extreme Learning Machines (ELM) approach. ELM is a neural network known 
for its auto-tuning capabilities. Assessed to various learning methods ELM demonstrates superior performance, faster 
processing speed, and reduced computational costs.
This specific neural network architecture consists of only one hidden layer, which seldom needs tuning. When con-
trasted with alternative ML approaches like SVM and Random Forest, ELM offers enhanced performance, speed, and 
minimal overhead. Additionally, ELM achieves better accuracy and improved results through the use of kernel functions. 
The intricate workings of ELM are elaborated in sources [23, 24].

3.5  Optimization of neural network hyper parameters
Hyper parameter tuning aims to recognize the optimal settings for an approach to minimize its complexity before training 
begins. In this study, the hyper parameters that need adjustment include the count of hidden layers, units within those 
layers, number of iterations, dropout rate and batch size. The Logistic Chaotic Aquila Optimization approach is utilized 
to fine-tune these parameters, elevating classification performance. The underlying principles of the Logistic Chaotic 
Aquila Optimization algorithm are outlined below.
3.5.1  Aquila optimization algorithm
Abualigah et al. in 2021 introduced a meta-heuristic technique based on the hunting strategies of eagle, which known 
for its agility and precision in capturing prey with powerful talons. The method mirrors four primary hunting approaches 
of the eagle: high soaring followed by a vertical dive, contour flight with brief glides, low flight with gradual descent, and 
terrestrial pursuit. Reflecting these strategies, the Aquila Optimizer (AO) algorithm comprises five key stages: “Initializa-
tion, Expanded Exploration, Narrowed Exploration, Expanded Exploitation, and Narrowed Exploitation. The transition 
from exploration to exploitation within the AO approach typically occurs based on a condition: if the current iteration is 
less than or equal two-thirds of the higher iteration, exploration is prioritized; otherwise, exploitation takes precedence”.
Step 1: Initialization
In the initial stage, the array of solutions has been created arbitrarily, while the remaining parameters of AO are set 
to their starting values.
Step 2: Expanded Exploration

to great heights by a vertical dive. The algorithms seek to determine the search rate from the lofty ascent, a concept 
encapsulated mathematically in Eq. (3).

3.5.1.1  Computational complexity  Computation complexity assessment for Algorithmic Optimization (AO) is signifi-
cantly influenced by several factors, including population size (n), initialization of individuals, fitness computation, and 
individual upgrades, along with the iterations count (T) and problem dimension (D). Initializing the population incurs 
a complexity of O(n). The complexity related to upgrading individuals is expressed as O(T*n) + O(T*n*D). Consequently, 
the overall time difficulty of AO is O(n*(T*(D + 1))). However, ascertaining the complexity of computation of such stochas-
tic approaches is notably challenging due to the unique search processes of Nature-Inspired Optimization Algorithms 
(NIOAs), which may not guarantee finding the global optimum within a designated timeframe. Hence, it’s been observed 
in academic literature that the temporal complexity of NIOAs is often assessed using theoretical CPU time.
3.5.1.2  Parameter sensitivity  The primary determinants influencing the exploitation capability of the AO are α and δ. In 
traditional AO methodologies, empirical assessments have been undertaken across ascertain the most advantageous 
settings for α and δ. Empirical findings indicate that AO yields optimal outcomes for extended durations when α and δ 
are assigned minimal values, such as 0.1. However, critiques highlight that while AO demonstrates considerable explora-
tion prowess, its exploitation capacity is hindered by the fixed initialization values for α and δ. Notably, the exploration 
efficacy of AO is heavily contingent upon the parameters governing the Lévy distribution.
Additionally, the authors assessed the impact of population size on AO’s performance. They found that both the size 
of the initial population and its composition significantly affect AO’s performance. Existing research has illustrated that 
maintaining a constant population size across various problem dimensions lacks scientific rigor and is referred to as the 
"population size curse." To address this, the literature suggests adjusting the population size to incorporate a balanced 
exploration–exploitation trade-off in any NIOA.

Figure 5, 6, 7, 8 displays the validation results of the DL model within a Fog environment, utilizing real-time datasets. 
These findings clearly demonstrate that the proposed model excels in anticipating heart disease within the Fog-BAN

In Fig. 9, it’s clear that LSTM and RNN models exhibited lower performance, Fig. 10 while the proposed model and GRU 
models showed the highest efficacy in cardiac attack anticipation. Figures 9 through 11 demonstrate that the efficiency of 
the other existing algorithms gradually decreases with additional testing datasets. In contrast, the suggested model main-
tains consistent efficiency even with an increasing dataset size. Particularly, when the dataset size grows from 20 to 40%, 
the suggested algorithm performance and GRU are notably similar. However, as shown in Fig. 11, the proposed algorithm 
surpasses the GRU when the dataset reaches 40%. These findings suggest that the proposed algorithm, that integrates 
“feed-forward networks optimized by Chaotic Hawk with self-attention-based GRU”, achieves best efficacy in identifying 
cardiac disease in a fog environment. To validate the effectiveness of this architecture, various metaheuristic algorithms, 
were combined with GRU networks. The performance of these combined frameworks is presented and analyzed in Table 4.
Table 4 clearly portrays that the recommended combination outperforms the varied approaches, thanks to the effec-
tive incorporation of various models through logistic methods.
4.4  Model construction duration evaluation
Table 5 presents the Model Building Times (MBT) for several algorithms across the datasets, with a focus on validation. 
Evaluating MBT is crucial as training duration is a key factor in determining a model’s ability to effectively diagnose 
cardiac conditions. This consideration directly impacts resource utilization and model performance. Thus, MBT plays 
a significant role in finding an optimal balance between computational demands and classifier efficiency. According 
to the Fig. 12, the average MBT for the proposed algorithm is 1.16 s, compared to 1.56 s for GRU, 2.08 s for LSTM, and 
2.45 s for RNN. This analysis demonstrates that the proposed model, with its 1.16-s training time, is well-positioned 
to create an efficient cardiac disease surveillance system. The proposed model significantly reduce latency without 
compromising accuracy, which is critical for real-time applications on resource-constrained fog and edge devices.

The categorization results of various algorithms, along with aforementioned parameters and stability indicators, are 
detailed in Tables 5 and 6 correspondingly.

4.6  Statistical outcome validation process
With the scope deep learning optimization, metaheuristic approaches require statistical validation to demonstrate model 
superiority. To effectively validate various models, it’s essential to meet three statistical criteria: “normality, independence, 
and homoscedasticity. Normality is evaluated utilizing the Shapiro–Wilk test”, which depicted in Fig. 15.
As illustrated in Fig. 15, all approaches yielded p-values below 0.05, indicating that the normality test was successfully 
met for each model. However, the proposed framework has exceeded expectations, demonstrating statistical superiority 
over all other existing frameworks and optimization techniques. This assessment can be employed on the identical dataset 
comprising the optimal results attained in each iteration of every metaheuristic algorithm. The results of each method can

5  Conclusion and future scope
This study introduces a cutting-edge intelligent healthcare system which utilizes fog computing technology to enhance 
its capabilities. It applies fog computing specifically to patients with heart conditions, using DL models to diagnose 
cardiac problems. By integrating Chaotic Aquila Optimized Feed Forward layers with Self Attention GRU, the recom-
mended model merges real-time data collection with advanced DL techniques. Additionally, the model’s processing 
time for medical data is assessed using MBT. To validate the efficacy of the recommended approach, it is compared with 
various modern deep learning models. These models are further validated with real-time data retrieved in an IoT-Fog-
BAN condition. The results demonstrate that the proposed system significantly surpasses various models, excelling in 
the BAN-IoT-Fog environment for cardiac disease identification.
Future developments will focus on implementing cost-effective strategies to maintain high Quality of Service (QoS) 
standards, including deploying the framework in clinical trials with IoT-enabled devices for real-time monitoring and 
analysis to enable faster diagnosis and improved patient management. Federated decentralized training methods, requir-
ing fewer hardware resources, could replace traditional methods, and the framework could be adapted for applications 
in automation, smart homes, and agriculture.

Abstract: Healthcare 4.0 is considered to be the most resilient technology with the integration of Internet of Things (IoT), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and 5G wireless communication. These Internet-enabled devices compile human data and deliver it to remote clinical centers for efficient diagnosis and treatment processes. Though sensor-driven devices have largely eased everyday lives, these healthcare systems have been suffering from various security breaches and data privacy problems. This evokes a need for designing intelligent systems to eradicate data breaches and privacy problems. This research presents a groundbreaking framework that uniquely combines privacy-preserving optimized deep learning to effectively diagnose cardiac troubles utilizing edge and fog computing devices. The recommended framework is tested with real-time datasets and employs federated learning for training the network. To ensure high prediction performance, Gated Aquila Optimized Deep Feedforward Networks (GAODP) are used to predict heart diseases. In the primary instance, information is acquired by the IoT sensors and stored in fog gateways. Subsequently, the federated mode of GAODP is adopted for the prediction of heart diseases. The ablation tests are conducted utilizing IoT nodes connected to medical sensors, with fog gateways implemented using Embedded Jetson Nano gadgets. Extensive evaluations are carried out using the gathered datasets, and performance metrics are examined and analyzed. The experimentation involves various traditional deep learning frameworks to prove the performance of privacy-preserving models. Moreover, the duration required to construct the model is calculated to confirm the recommended model’s intricacy. The outcome indicate that the recommended model has attained notable predictive accuracy, including precision (0.98), recall (0.975), specificity (0.98), F1-score (0.99) and accuracy (0.99) with less computational overhead.
